title: Fast Synergetic Simulation to Study Slow Evolution of Soliton Patterns in Optical Resonators
authors: Sanzida Akter, Pradyoth Shandilya, Logan Courtright, Amir Leshem, Giuseppe D'Aguanno, Omri Gat, Curtis R. Menyuk
abstract: Complex patterns in physical and biological systems often emerge through slow collective dynamics governed by a small number of key variables. In nonlinear optical resonators, dissipative Kerr solitons provide an important example, where interactions between well-separated solitons can evolve over timescales far longer than the characteristic loss and gain timescales. Direct numerical simulation of these dynamics is challenging because stiffness forces conventional methods to resolve many rapidly damped degrees-of-freedom with very small time steps. We present a numerical scheme, the synergetic method, that eliminates these rapidly damped degrees-of-freedom and retains the slowly evolving modes, enabling time steps many orders of magnitude larger than those used in conventional approaches. Applied to soliton molecules in driven Kerr cavities, the method achieves speedups of $10^3$ to $10^5$ while capturing dynamics on laboratory timescales. We use it to model the full interaction dynamics of a three-soliton molecule and the evolution of an eight-soliton molecule. The approach provides an efficient framework for studying slow pattern formation in nonlinear systems with widely separated timescales.
summary: This paper introduces the synergetic method, a novel numerical technique designed to overcome the computational stiffness encountered when simulating systems with widely separated timescales. By projecting the dynamics onto the slowly evolving modes, the method efficiently models the long-term interaction and pattern formation of solitons in optical resonators, enabling simulations on realistic laboratory timescales.
main_problem: The primary challenge is numerically simulating the slow, long-term evolution of complex soliton patterns in optical resonators, where the dynamics are governed by timescales vastly different from the rapid damping timescales.
main_result: The authors developed and applied the 'synergetic method' to simulate multi-soliton interactions, achieving speedups of $10^3$ to $10^5$ times over conventional methods and modeling dynamics on laboratory timescales.
method: The synergetic method, inspired by Haken's framework, eliminates rapidly damped degrees-of-freedom by analyzing the Jacobian of the evolution equation, projecting the dynamics onto the slow, dominant eigenmodes.
model_or_system: The system is based on dissipative Kerr solitons in a driven nonlinear Kerr cavity, modeled by the Lugiato-Lefever equation (a driven-damped nonlinear Schrödinger equation).
key_observables: Inter-soliton separations ($p_1, p_2$), the potential function $U(p_1, p_2)$, and the dynamical spectrum (eigenvalues) of the linearized operator.
important_parameters: The separation between fast (damping) and slow (pattern evolution) timescales, and the ability to simulate dynamics over laboratory timescales (e.g., seconds).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the long-term behavior is governed by a small cluster of eigenvalues near zero, corresponding to the slow collective dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the system's dynamics, showing the evolution of soliton patterns (single, molecule, crystal) and mapping the potential energy landscape $U(p_1, p_2)$ that governs the slow convergence of the system.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical context (solitons in microresonators), identifies the computational bottleneck (stiffness due to timescale separation), proposes the synergetic method based on Jacobian analysis, and validates it by simulating complex multi-soliton interactions and mapping their potential energy surfaces.
why_interesting: This work presents a powerful, generalizable numerical technique for analyzing complex, slow dynamics in nonlinear physical systems, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and nonlinear wave physics.

A microring resonator is driven by an external CW laser source to generate a train of soliton pulses or more complex patterns that form a frequency comb, as analyzed using an optical spectrum analyzer. (b) Intracavity intensity profile illustration of commonly observed optical patterns. Anomalous dispersion regime: (i) a single dissipative Kerr soliton, (ii) a soliton molecule, (iii) a perfect soliton crystal. Normal dispersion regime: (iv) a dark soliton.

Figure 2: (a) (i) Profile of a single soliton stationary solution. (ii) The corresponding eigenvalue spectrum derived from the linearized operator. The spectrum reveals a fourfold symmetry and a single eigenvalue near zero, corresponding to translational invariance of the soliton. (b) (i) A three- soliton molecule solution and (ii) its eigenvalue profile. Here, there are three eigenvalues near zero: one represents translational invariance (similar to the single soliton), while the other two represent the slowly varying DOFs associated with the relative motion between solitons.
